lignes.texte: Deep in the heart of Texas lies a multi-million dollar graveyard.
It’s not filled with bodies… it’s packed with endless rows of abandoned $80,000
trucks. Right now, American auto loans are surging past 2008 financial crisis records.
And it’s not slowing down. It’s all fueled by a predatory
illusion engineered by banks and dealerships to trick American drivers. Now those
luxury vehicles are gathering dust in lots. The banks don’t care about the circumstances.
They don’t care about the families. All they want are the keys.
And it affects you… In 2024 alone, a staggering
1.7 million vehicles were repossessed in the U.S. That’s a number nearly equal to the amount of cars
driving around New York city. It’s a genuine crisis.
And it’s accelerating. Texas leads the way with almost
320,000 repossessions in the first three quarters of 2025. Florida follows closely,
with 222,000repos in the same period. So how did so many Americans end up
with vehicles they couldn’t afford. It’s the result of a perfect storm:
dealer tricks, skyrocketing car prices, and shady loan structures. Together,
they have led to a massive auto loan debt of $1.7 trillion. That’s more than the entire annual GDP
of Turkiye. It’s also more than twice the level of outstanding auto debt recorded in 2010,
at the peak of the Great Recession. And the suburbs are taking the hit.
According to the American Counseling Consumer Credit Organization, the average person calling
them up for help with consumer debt used to make around $50,000 a year. In 2024-2025, the average
person struggling under mountains of crushing consumer debt makes around $75,000 a year.
The middle class is drowning in debt. It makes sense when you look at the
numbers. Since 2019, the price of a new car has gone up by 35%. Today,
the average new car in the U.S. has now breached $50,000. For the everyday American, buying a car
means sacrificing their entire post tax income. When it comes to trucks – the US’ most popular
vehicles - the increase has been even steeper. According to Cox Automotive, the
average full-size truck now costs almost $65,000. The average monthly payment on a new car loan is
$761. Used cars don’t fare much better, racking up an average of $570 a month in payments. Compared
to 2019, that’s almost a $300-a-month increase. And that’s not even the worst part.
Data from credit agency Experian reveals that almost 1 in 5 new vehicle loans have monthly
payments of over $1,000. In 2021, it was only 5.4%. These payments aren’t for high-end models
or luxury vehicles either. 74% of those thousand dollar loans are for standard non-luxury vehicles.
They’re mostly pickup trucks, including the Chevy Silverado 1500 and the Ford F-150.
How are families affording these new cars during rapid inflation and low wage growth?
They aren’t. But auto dealers
have a way around that. A sleight of hand that fools people into signing on the dotted line.
The 84-month loan. 7 years of car payments.
This is a relatively recent financial instrument engineered by lenders and offered by dealerships
to make surging vehicle prices more palatable to the average consumer. The average amount
consumers need to borrow is now up to $44,000. So 7 years of relatively lower payments sounds
relatively appealing. But it destroys their
long term financial survival. Major platforms like Carvana
approve loans for people making as little as $5,000 a year. They’re handing the keys
to people making around $100 per week, then acting surprised when that person defaults.
Dealers want to sell cars. They want to close the deal.
And it’s working. Loans of 72 months or longer make up 27.5% of the market.
Almost 1 in 3 Americans are signing up for a never-ending, interest-heavy debt burden.
Statistically, it’s going to drag them under. Edmunds director of insights, Ivan Drury,
put it simply: “as vehicles become increasingly more expensive,
[84-month auto loans] will be used more often.” But many consumers don't understand how much these
loans are costing them. If a car buyer took out a $40,000 loan over a period of 60 months, they
would end up paying just over $7,500 in interest. If they took out the same loan over 84 months, the
total interest paid shoots up to around $10,700. They’re handing over thousands of dollars more
based on an illusion of lower monthly payments. The financial bleeding doesn’t stop there.
Most manufacturer warranties expire after 2 to 3 years. On an 84 month loan, the warranty will
run out while there’s still 5 years of payments left. If there’s a major breakdown or repair,
it’s coming out of their pocket. All the while, the car is
depreciating while the debt stays alive. Kelley Blue Book states that the average
new car loses 30% of its value within the first 2 years of buying it. The percentage is
even higher for luxury cars and trucks. After that, it loses 8-12% of its value every year.
For people who have 7-year loans to pay off, this steep drop in value is a massive problem.
In just two years, they can find themselves owing more than the car is worth. Not only
does this mean selling at a loss if something comes up and a consumer needs to sell their
car. It also means consumers are less likely to make their payments in the first place.
The Texas Standard states, “the incentive for a car buyer to pay and make a missed monthly
payment decreases when the vehicle’s value is below the outstanding balance.” It starts
a vicious cycle. Missing car payments increases the chances of a buyer’s car
getting repossessed by the bank. And the buyer then takes a massive loss on their purchase.
At least if the bank takes it back, the loan is finally off your hands, right?
Wrong. Some consumers don’t
even know it until their car is lifted from their driveway, and they get a bill for everything they
still owe. The bank takes your truck, sells it for pennies, and bills you for the rest.
As of December 2022, the average outstanding balance a consumer owed after a repossession
was up to $11,000. That doesn’t even touch on the money the consumer owes lenders for
the repossession itself, which can range from hundreds of dollars to a couple of thousands.
But when it comes to repo, the banks are getting their hands dirty.
Lenders are increasingly using third-party repossession forwarding companies to track
down delinquent owners. They handled 66% of cases in December 2022 compared to 31% of cases
in January 2018. The middle men charge higher rates which get tacked onto the car owner’s bill.
So losing your vehicle is even more expensive. And the repo men are busier than ever.
Between 2022 and 2024, vehicle repos increased by 43%. Even though the car is no longer in your
driveway, the fallout looms over you for years. Being delinquent, or worse yet, defaulting on
car payments affects a consumer’s credit score, including their ability to secure a car loan - or
any loan - in the future. And repossessions can stay on credit reports for up to 7 years;
also affecting future auto insurance rates. The less able you are to make payments now,
the less likely it is you will ever be able to afford car payments and insurance in the future.
It’s why this particular bubble is so dangerous. Even if the car doesn’t get repo’d, and the
consumer just trades it in for another vehicle, all that negative equity starts them off in the
red. It’s not a rare event anymore. Edmunds found that 1 in 3 car buyers are carrying
negative equity when trading in for a new vehicle. In spring of 2024, only 23.9% of car buyers had
negative equity. A year earlier, that share was as low as 18.5%. The rapid increase in car buyers
operating in the red has experts very worried. Maybe that’s why the U.S. Automotive Financing
Satisfaction Study found that 29% of auto finance customers are now categorized as
“financially vulnerable”. The average amount of that equity is $7,200 in the red. For trucks,
that number goes up past $10,000. It’s an all time high.
Rolling $11,000 of negative equity into a new truck is the mathematical equivalent of buying
a reliable used car and immediately pushing it off a cliff before you even drive off the lot.
Edmunds’ Jessica Caldwell says, “consumers owing a grand or two more than their cars are worth isn’t
the end of the world, but seeing such a notable share of individuals affected at the $10,000 or
even $15,000 level is nothing short of alarming…” But is this solely the consumer’s fault?
Banks have figured out a way to turn your debt into pure profit. It’s driven by a Wall Street
trick known as Asset Backed Securities, or ABS. Lenders take thousands of high risk auto
loans and pool them together. They then sell them off to global investors as bonds. The
investors get a steady stream of income from your payments and the banks get an immediate payout.
If it sounds terrifyingly familiar, that’s because it is.
It’s the same play that triggered the 2008 financial crisis. Wall Street failed to learn
its lesson… or it just doesn’t care. They're killing off subprime auto ABS,
completely ignoring the warning signs. But this time, there’s a fatal flaw.
Unlike houses, cars are rapidly depreciating assets. They lose value quickly, and loans
mature over a few years at most. That means when consumers start defaulting on loans,
not only will the defaults start coming in fast; but the assets won’t even be worth much.
In fact, according to one law firm that deals with repo cases, “when a vehicle is repossessed
and sold, the sale price often does not cover the remaining loan balance.” The difference between
what a consumer owes on a car loan and what the bank sold is called a “deficiency balance.”
It’s classified as unsecured debt. Lenders will try to collect it directly after selling off your
car. If you don’t pay immediately, it gets transferred to a third-party debt collector.
If you can’t pay the debt collector in a timely manner, lenders can sue to take
the money directly out of your wages. The only way the consumer can truly
get out of paying the deficiency balance is to declare Chapter 7 bankruptcy. Which most
people don’t prefer for a whole host of reasons. But in the meantime, financial companies make a
lot of money. A huge chunk of subprime auto loans were wrapped into an ABS known as Drive 2019-3.
Investment firms took on these securities - which included over 75,000 auto loans - because clever
financial maneuvering made Drive 2019-3 pay out higher yields than Treasury bonds.
That’s partly because of the exorbitant rates companies can charge when giving loans to people
with poor credit. Santander Consumer USA charged one consumer, Janice Siler, 22.05% interest on
her loan to buy a used car. A customer with good credit would get a rate more than 3 times lower.
Even when she defaults, it’s not a big deal for Santander and Co. They built
their securities based on the assumption that up to 42% of customers could and would default,
and their bottom line would remain unaffected. How can the companies do this?
By allegedly fudging the numbers. In Siler’s case, Santander gave her the loan based on
Janice making an annual income of $70,000 a year. But Janice never made that much.
And she never told Santander that she did. As Daniel Chu, CEO of subprime auto lender
Tricolor Holdings says, “it doesn’t really work for the consumer. But it works for everyone else”.
And thanks to creative financial instruments and usurious interest rates, the subprime auto ABS
market is booming. According to Bloomberg, as of 2022, subprime auto loans backed more
than $37 billion in bonds. In 2012, the value of the subprime auto ABS market was just half that.
Just like with subprime mortgage loans, it’s all going great…
Until it isn’t. The average consumer is left
holding the bag while the financial giants have made off with billions. In the subprime
auto ABS market, the red flags are starting to show; because the dominoes are already falling.
The first one? Tricolor Holdings. Tricolor was a big “buy here, pay
here” – known as BHPH - dealership chain operating in Texas, Arizona, and California. Customers would
get both their used cars and subprime loans in the same place. Many of these buyers were customers
who could not get a car loan through traditional financial institutions because of poor credit.
In May 2025, the Federal Reserve actually found that 78% of BHPH
customers were subprime borrowers, compared to 27% of customers for regular auto lenders.
But Tricolor was giving out loans to people it knew would never be able to pay them off. Overall,
BHPH loans have 1.88 times the default rates of traditional auto loans, and 2.65 times the
delinquency rates. The rate of repossessions for BHPH customers was 16.6 times the rate of
repossessions for the average car consumers. It amounted to around 5% of BHPH balances.
Defaults hit such high that not only did the company declare bankruptcy in September 2025;
the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has charged Tricolor executives with
fraud. That includes the formerly quoted Daniel Chu. as well as CFO Jerome Kollar
and Senior Director of Finance Ameryn Seibold. Apparently, Tricolor had “an alleged multi-year
scheme to defraud investors by double pledging hundreds of millions of dollars of subprime
auto loans to multiple asset-backed securities (ABS) offerings and lenders.”
The bankruptcy of the company caused the two major banks who were providing credit lines to Tricolor
to lose between tens of millions and hundreds of millions each. These range from local Louisiana
banks like Origin Bancorp., to major international institutions like JPMorgan Chase and Barclays. But
even though Tricolor may have gone under, the subprime auto loan market is still thriving...
At the expense of everyday consumers. Overall, when it comes to subprime borrowers,
almost 16% were at least 30 days past due on their car payments as of late 2025. Prime borrowers,
though they have lower delinquency rates, are also feeling the crunch, as an affordability
crisis lessens their ability to pay. But lenders often look at something called
delinquency roll-rates to see just how badly the market is shifting. Anyone can miss one car
payment, by accident or because of an unexpected cost eating into their budget. A delinquency
roll-rate looks at how many consumers go from one missed payment… to two. Then three. Then more.
The bad news is, 60-day delinquency rates are faring worse than they used to as well.
In January 2025, 6.9% of consumers with subprime auto loans were at least 2 full billing schedules
past due on their scheduled car payments. As for U.S. auto loan 90+ day delinquencies?
They have now reached 5.2%. While that may not sound like much, it’s actually way above the norm.
Coming with 0.06 percentage points of defaults during the peak of the 2010 Great Recession.
Before then, the rates of over-90-day delinquency usually hovered around 2%. The outstanding balance
owed today is $1.66 trillion. That’s double the outstanding balance of 2010.
These delinquencies and repossessions are also wreaking havoc on the used car market. Though
for consumers burdened by high costs, it may be the one bright spot in the current auto industry.
Auto news outlets predict that used-vehicle values could drop up to 4% in 2026 compared to
the year before. While that’s a reflection of lower-than-usual consumer confidence,
another factor may also be the hundreds of thousands of repossessed
vehicles flooding the market at low, low prices. The bigger problem for the average U.S. consumer?
Defaults on these car loans can affect you… even if you’re not the one that holds them.
If your retirement or pension fund is invested in subprime auto ABS,
and the securities collapse, it’s your retirement money that’s going to be caught in the crossfires.
Depending on where you live and what your company pension funds invest in,
the exposure can be pretty significant. 15% of the Arizona State Retirement system’s portfolio
goes to private credit. Another 7% is invested in distressed debt. California Public Employees’
Retirement System is also making investments in private credit, passing 5% investment as of 2022.
According to the Wall Street Journal, “across the U.S., state and local retirement funds with
private-credit portfolios are expanding them faster than any other alternative investment,
from an average allocation of 3% to an average target of 5.7%”.
Most consumers aren’t entirely sure if these private credit investments, including the ones
that control their own pension funds, are going to risky funds like subprime auto securities.
So when it comes to the question of how Americans are affording
$80,000 trucks on a $70,000 salary these days, the ugly truth is… they’re not.
The auto and lending industries have led them to believe that it’s possible with shady financial
and lending practices. Increasing car costs are only adding to the pressures and mounting debt.
But when payment comes due, it could bring the whole economy crashing down.
Consumers might be feeling the effects of shady practices, but that doesn’t mean the
auto manufacturers are safe. Watch “REAL Reason Why FORD Is Failing” to see why
one of the biggest names in automotive history is imploding. Or click on this.
